case.case_title: A. R. Perera & Others vs Central Freight Bureau of Sri Lanka and Another
case.court_name: Court of Appeal of Sri Lanka
case.source_citation: Sri Lanka Law Reports (2006) 1 Sri L R. 83

clause.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioners, as office bearers and members of CASA and a corporate shipping agent, have locus standi to challenge the imposition of levies and service charges by the respondent, invoking Article 12(1) rights.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioners argued that they have sufficient interest and locus standi to file the application on behalf of CASA members and in their personal capacities, asserting that the imposition of levies affects their fundamental rights including equality before the law.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondent contended that the petitioners lack locus standi as CASA is a corporate body with the power to sue and be sued, and only CASA as a company can maintain the application, not the individual office bearers or members. They argued the petitioners are mere 'busy bodies' without legal standing.
key_facts: CASA is a company limited by guarantee with 113 members who are shipping agents.
The Executive Committee of CASA resolved that the petitioners should file the application on behalf of its membership.
The petitioners include the Chairman, Secretary General of CASA, and a member of the Executive Committee who is also a director/shareholder of a shipping agent company.
The respondent imposed levies and service charges which the petitioners challenge.
The respondent raised a preliminary objection on locus standi grounds.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court interpreted Article 12(1) as guaranteeing equality before the law and equal protection, which supports a liberal approach to locus standi, allowing persons whose interests are affected to seek judicial review even if the grievance is shared by many. The court emphasized that the petitioners have a sufficient interest and are not mere busy bodies.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The court found that the petitioners, as office bearers and members of CASA and representatives of affected shipping agents, have a genuine grievance and sufficient interest to maintain the application. The court rejected the narrow, conservative view that only the corporate body can sue, recognizing the petitioners' standing under the constitutional guarantee of equality and access to justice.
principles_established: Locus standi rules have evolved to be more liberal, especially in public law matters involving fundamental rights.
Persons affected by governmental actions, even if the grievance is shared by many, have standing to seek judicial review.
Corporate bodies have legal personality, but individuals representing affected members may also have standing.
The constitutional right to equality before the law supports access to courts for affected persons.
The concept of 'busy bodies' is rejected where genuine interest and grievance exist.

outcome.holding: The court overruled the preliminary objection and held that the petitioners have sufficient locus standi to maintain the application, recognizing their right to seek relief under Article 12(1).
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Preliminary objection on locus standi dismissed; matter set down for argument on merits.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(1) was central to the court's reasoning on locus standi, as the constitutional guarantee of equality before the law and equal protection underpins the liberal approach to standing and access to judicial remedies.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The court emphasized that the petitioners are persons whose interests are affected and have sufficient interest to distinguish them from mere busy bodies, citing Article 12(1) rights to equal protection and access to courts.
